parsed_answer.content: In computer science, pass-by-value and pass-by-reference define how arguments are passed to functions. Pass-by-value means the actual value of the argument is copied into the function's local parameter, meaning changes to the parameter inside the function do not affect the original variable. Pass-by-reference means the function receives a direct alias or memory address to the original variable, allowing the function to modify the caller's data directly. Java is strictly pass-by-value. When you pass a primitive type, the literal value is copied. When you pass an object, you are passing the value of the reference—essentially a copy of the memory address pointing to the object on the heap. This is often confused with pass-by-reference because you can modify the object's internal state via its methods, but you cannot change the reference itself to point to a new object in the caller's scope.

items: When an object is passed, Java creates a copy of the reference variable (the pointer to the heap address) and passes that copy to the method stack frame.

Because the reference is copied, reassigning the parameter variable (e.g., 'obj = new Object()') inside a method only updates the local copy, leaving the original reference in the calling method untouched.
Mutating the object (e.g., 'obj.setName("New")') works because both the original reference and the copied reference point to the same heap memory location.
Primitive types (int, boolean, etc.) are stored directly on the stack; passing them copies the actual bits, ensuring total isolation between the caller and the callee.

parsed_answer.content: A common trap for junior developers is assuming that because they can modify an object's state, Java is 'pass-by-reference'. Always remember: if you can't swap the caller's variable to point to a different instance, it is not pass-by-reference. If you need to return a new object from a method, you must return it explicitly or wrap it in a container object, as the reference itself is passed by value.
